result:
**Recommendation: REST** (JSON over HTTP, described with OpenAPI). For a new public API it is the safer default, and GraphQL is worth it only if specific conditions hold.

| Concern | REST | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|
| Consumer familiarity | Universal; works with curl and any HTTP client | Requires learning the query language and usually a client library |
| Caching | HTTP caching, CDNs and ETags work out of the box | Mostly POSTs to one endpoint; needs persisted queries or client-side caches |
| Rate limiting and abuse control | Simple: per endpoint, per request | Hard: needs query cost analysis, depth limits and complexity budgets |
| Fetching flexibility | Fixed shapes; can over-fetch or need multiple round trips | Client picks exactly the fields and nested relations it needs in one request |
| Evolution | Explicit versioning; breaking changes are visible | Additive evolution with field deprecation; no versions, but removal is slow |
| Typing and docs | Good with OpenAPI, but the spec can drift from the code | Schema is the contract; introspection and tooling are excellent |
| Performance risk | Predictable per endpoint | N+1 resolvers and expensive arbitrary queries need active defence |
| Observability and errors | Status codes, per-route metrics, standard tooling | Often 200 with errors in the body; needs per-field instrumentation |
| File uploads, webhooks, streaming | Native or well-established patterns | Bolt-ons |

**Why REST for a public API**

- **Lowest integration friction.** You do not control the clients, and every language, tool and developer already speaks HTTP and JSON.
- **Cheaper to operate safely.** With anonymous third parties, predictable per-endpoint cost matters more than query flexibility. GraphQL lets strangers compose arbitrarily expensive queries unless you build a cost model.
- **Caching and infrastructure come for free.** CDNs, gateways, auth proxies and monitoring all understand REST semantics.
- **Its weak spots are patchable.** Sparse fieldsets (`?fields=`), `?include=` expansions, cursor pagination and SDKs generated from OpenAPI cover most over-fetching and typing complaints.

**When I'd pick GraphQL instead**

- The data is a deeply connected graph and consumers need very different slices of it (GitHub and Shopify are the examples).
- The main consumers are rich front ends or mobile apps where round trips and payload size dominate.
- You have the team capacity to build query cost limiting, dataloaders and persisted queries from day one.

If you later find a real need, adding GraphQL on top of a well-designed REST API is a much easier path than the reverse.

If you tell me who the consumers are and what the data model looks like, I can check whether any of those GraphQL conditions apply to you.
